claims.summary: Roll out new Pods for A; leave B and C running. — Rolling out A is the documented way to refresh A’s startup-consumed environment, but leaving B unchanged does not refresh its pre-update subPath mount. This exact selective action is appropriate when A alone still needs refreshing and B has already received the current ConfigMap in a replacement Pod, while C is already current. It makes no claim that B’s existing subPath file can update automatically.

Roll out new Pods for B; leave A and C running. — Rolling out B recreates its Pod and configuration mount, but leaving A unchanged preserves A’s pre-update process environment. This exact selective action is appropriate when B alone remains outdated and A has already started replacement Pods with the current ConfigMap, while C is already current. It does not claim that A’s running process environment refreshes itself.

Roll out new Pods for A and B; leave C running. — The frozen ConfigMap unit distinguishes startup environment values and subPath mounts, which do not auto-refresh, from ordinary updating volumes. Replacing the pre-update Pods for A and B obtains current configuration, while C’s observed updated file and per-request reread satisfy the no-C-rollout requirement.

Roll out new Pods for A, B, and C. — A rollout of every Deployment is a valid way to refresh all startup-consumed configuration when every application requires new Pods and no keep-running constraint excludes one. Here C already has and consumes the updated file, and replacing C violates the explicit requirement to keep it running. The action is valid, but its scope is unnecessarily broad for this task.

sourceReviews.supportingSummary: Freshly reread the complete frozen ConfigMap unit for v3. It explicitly documents startup environment initialization from the current ConfigMap, no automatic environment refresh, the subPath auto-update exception, ordinary volume updates and application-specific consumption. These support refreshing A/B while C needs no refresh. The unit does not equate lack of necessity with a prohibition on C Pod replacement or establish that every full rollout stops an application.

choiceReviews.rationale: New Pods for A legitimately refresh its startup environment. Leaving B running preserves its pre-update subPath projection, so this exact partial action does not update all stated consumers. The literal action would suffice if B had already received the current configuration through replacement Pods and only A remained stale; this changes prior state, not B consumption mode or an auto-refresh claim.

New Pods for B recreate its configuration mount, but leaving pre-update A running retains A startup environment. This exact selective action would fit B as the only remaining stale consumer after A had already started replacement Pods with current configuration. No process-environment auto-update or ordinary-volume substitution is needed to establish that valid context.

The documented projection rules require new Pods for the stale startup-environment and subPath consumers A/B. C already has the changed ordinary-volume file and rereads it, so leaving C untouched is sufficient and avoids an unnecessary rollout. This is the supported minimal plan; the concern is whether the stem unambiguously excludes the broader d plan, not whether c works.

Replacing all three Pod sets is a genuine way to reinitialize configuration and is appropriate when all consumers need replacement or a full rollout is permitted. The source proves that C does not need new Pods, not that replacing its Pods necessarily makes the application stop running. The actual stem requires keeping C running but does not explicitly forbid a C Pod rollout or require the existing C Pods to remain untouched. Therefore the authored explanation imports a stronger no-C-rollout constraint than the stem supplies, leaving this alternative insufficiently excluded.

review.verificationNotes: Fresh same-context pass-2 review of the exact v3 stem, four literal actions, complete explanations and actual ConfigMap evidence. The earlier a/b impossible automatic-refresh defect is resolved: each now has a valid prior-state countercontext without changing environment/subPath mode. Key c is supported as the necessary minimal refresh. Retain a manual hold because keeping C running does not explicitly prohibit new C Pods; the explanation treats an unstated no-C-rollout rule as explicit to reject d. Require a precise existing-C-Pod/no-replacement constraint (or an explicit minimum-required-rollout rule) in the authored stem. No old approval is inherited and no v1/v2 record is changed.

Complete answer uniqueness remains unresolved because source evidence establishes that C replacement is unnecessary, while the wording does not clearly prohibit it. This is a focused repairable scope hold, not a false-key or source-provenance rejection.
